article_title: Profiles and Transitions of Psychological Adaptation in AI-Assisted Japanese Language Learning
citation: Wu Y (2026) Proﬁles and transitions of psychological adaptation in AI-assisted Japanese language learning. Front. Psychol. 17:1837484. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1837484
title: Job Demands–Resources-based demand–resource configuration account of psychological adaptation to AI-assisted language learning
description: The article draws on Job Demands–Resources theory to give its three latent profiles substantive meaning: technostress is treated as a context-specific demand and resilience as a personal resource, so adaptation is "a person-speciﬁc demand–resource conﬁguration." A demand-dominant configuration (high technostress, low resilience) reflects vulnerability to maladaptation, a resource-advantaged configuration (low technostress, high resilience) reflects positive adaptation, and intermediate configurations reflect a tentative balance. The framework also links the profiles to a health-impairment pathway (burnout) and a resource-supported motivational pathway (self-efficacy).
requirements: Both a demand indicator (technostress) and a resource indicator (resilience) must be measured jointly, since adaptation is defined by their configuration rather than either construct alone
constraints: The article states the number and configuration of profiles were not specified in advance, so outcome differences were examined through research questions rather than directional hypotheses
target_learners: tertiary-level learners of Japanese using AI-based tools
target_learning_goals: sustaining psychological adaptation, self-efficacy, and wellbeing in AI-assisted language learning
examples: Latent profile analyses across three waves identified maladaptive, moderate, and positive adaptation profiles whose proportions shifted toward more adaptive configurations over the semester
key_sources: Wu Y (2026) Proﬁles and transitions of psychological adaptation in AI-assisted Japanese language learning. Front. Psychol. 17:1837484. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1837484

article_title: Professional learning of late-career teachers: A systematic literature review
citation: Brouhier, Q., Raemdonck, I., & März, V. (2026). Professional Learning of Late-career Teachers: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review, 50, 100757. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100757
title: Job Demands-Resources model as an organising framework for late-career teachers' engagement in professional learning
description: The review structures its analysis around the Job Demands-Resources model, using it to categorise the workplace conditions that influence late-career teachers' engagement in learning. Job demands named include "workload, role ambiguity"; resources include "collegial support, autonomy, self-efficacy". The model thus organises how demands and resources shape whether teachers aged 50 and above engage in professional learning across the reviewed studies.
requirements: Applicable to analysing professional learning contexts where both job demands and job resources can be identified for late-career teachers
target_learning_goals: Sustained engagement in professional learning in the later stages of teaching careers
examples: The review categorises key job demands (e.g., workload, role ambiguity) and resources (e.g., collegial support, autonomy, self-efficacy) influencing late-career teachers' engagement in learning.
key_sources: Brouhier, Q., Raemdonck, I., & März, V. (2026). Professional Learning of Late-career Teachers: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review, 50, 100757. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100757

article_title: Factors Associated with Teacher Wellbeing: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Sijing Zhou, Gavin R. Slemp & Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick. (2024). Factors Associated with Teacher Wellbeing: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09886-x
title: Job Demands-Resources theory as a framework for classifying antecedents, consequences, and correlates of teacher wellbeing
description: The article uses JD-R theory to position factors in the nomological network of teacher wellbeing. The theory "proposes that job-related phenomena can be modelled using two broad categories: job demands and job resources," with demands activating a health impairment process and resources a motivational process, plus personal resources as aspects of the self. The authors build a conceptual model (Fig. 1) grouping antecedents into individual differences and personal characteristics, interpersonal characteristics, and workplace characteristics, with correlates and consequences classified separately.
requirements: Requires distinguishing wellbeing (hedonic, eudaimonic, general, occupational) from its exogenous antecedents and endogenous consequences, excluding models that conflate them
constraints: The article notes moderator results may highlight boundary conditions of JD-R theory, and moderator analyses were exploratory
target_learning_goals: informing school leadership and policy practice
examples: The meta-analysis coded 173 studies' correlates into JD-R-based antecedent, consequence, and correlate categories and meta-analyzed each association corrected for sampling and measurement error
key_sources: Sijing Zhou, Gavin R. Slemp & Dianne A. Vella-Brodrick. (2024). Factors Associated with Teacher Wellbeing: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09886-x

article_title: University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement
citation: Martin Andrew J., Ginns Paul, Collie Rebecca J. (2023). University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101712
title: Job Demands-Resources theory and its academic adaptation, the Academic Demands-Resources (AD-R) model
description: JD-R theory holds that contextual demands (aspects of work "that require physical and/or psychological exertion") and resources (aspects supporting goal attainment) predict motivation and performance, alongside modifiable personal resources; it also posits buffering and boosting moderation effects. The AD-R model adapts these processes to students' academic experience. The study operationalizes lockdown as demand, adaptability and fluid reasoning as personal resources, self-efficacy as motivation, and engagement/disengagement as outcomes.
requirements: Demands, resources, motivation, and outcomes must be measured so main effects and moderation (interaction) terms can be modeled
constraints: The article notes demands and resources can be appraised differently by individuals, so effects may vary in sign or size across students
examples: The study modeled lockdown status, perceived adaptability, and fluid reasoning as predictors of self-efficacy, which in turn predicted participation, aspirations, enjoyment, and disengagement
key_sources: Martin Andrew J., Ginns Paul, Collie Rebecca J. (2023). University students in COVID-19 lockdown: The role of adaptability and fluid reasoning in supporting their academic motivation and engagement. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101712

article_title: Dual Pathways From Self-Compassion and Self-Criticism to Academic Achievement: The Roles of Engagement and Exhaustion.
citation: Consiglio P, Fokkens-Bruinsma M, Opdenakker M-C, Jansen EPWA, Fleer J. (2026). Dual Pathways From Self-Compassion and Self-Criticism to Academic Achievement: The Roles of Engagement and Exhaustion. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1821
title: Job Demands–Resources Model applied to medical education: bright and dark pathways from personal resources and demands to achievement
description: The study applies the Job Demands–Resources model, in which "burnout and engagement [are] distinct constructs encompassed within two key processes": a motivational process in which personal resources such as self-compassion foster engagement and favourable outcomes, and a health impairment process in which personal demands such as self-criticism drive burnout symptoms and diminished achievement. The study tested these as 'bright' and 'dark' pathways with engagement and exhaustion as mediators and GPA as an objective outcome.
requirements: Measurement of personal resources and demands alongside engagement, exhaustion and an objective achievement outcome over time.
constraints: The authors note they did not test the full JD-R model, which would require incorporating study demands and resources such as workload, institutional culture and financial stressors.
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting academic achievement, engagement and well-being
examples: The study operationalised the model with self-compassion as a personal resource, self-criticism as a personal demand, engagement and exhaustion as mediators, and averaged exam grades as objective achievement.
key_sources: Consiglio P, Fokkens-Bruinsma M, Opdenakker M-C, Jansen EPWA, Fleer J. (2026). Dual Pathways From Self-Compassion and Self-Criticism to Academic Achievement: The Roles of Engagement and Exhaustion. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.1821

article_title: Comparing the Effectiveness of Multimodal Learning Using Computer-Based and Immersive Virtual Reality Simulation-Based Interprofessional Education With Co-Debriefing, Medical Movies, and Massive Online Open Courses for Mitigating Stress and Long-Term Burnout in Medical Training: Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Lesselroth Blake, Nooripour Roghieh, Srikasem Sirikanyawan MSc, Seephom Sunisa PhD, Viriyopase Atthaphon PhD, Phutrakool Phanupong PhD, Khowinthaseth Sirhavich MD, Narajeenron Khuansiri MD, MSc, CHSE, MHPE, ER-VIPE Study Group. (2025). Comparing the Effectiveness of Multimodal Learning Using Computer-Based and Immersive Virtual Reality Simulation–Based Interprofessional Education With Co-Debriefing, Medical Movies, and Massive Online Open Courses for Mitigating Stress and Long-Term Burnout in Medical Training: Quasi-Experimental Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/70726
title: Job Demands-Resources model as the burnout mechanism account guiding the ER-VIPE intervention
description: The article adopts the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, one of what it calls the 2 leading theoretical frameworks on burnout, to explain both how prolonged occupational distress produces burnout and why the intervention should work. According to the model, "burnout occurs when the availability of resources—both job-related (eg, knowledge, skills, abilities, social support) and personal (eg, self-efficacy)—is insufficient over time to buffer the negative effects of job demands on individual strain." Increasing access to physical, psychological, social, or organizational resources can mitigate burnout risk; the authors position co-debriefing resources (psychosocial support, teamwork, learning) as such buffers.
requirements: Resources of the four kinds the model names (job-related and personal) must be available to buffer job demands
constraints: The model is presented as a hypothesis about buffering, not as a tested mediation result of this study
target_learning_goals: understanding and mitigating occupational stress and burnout in emergency care training
examples: The authors frame debriefing's psychosocial support, teamwork improvement, and learning gains as job and personal resources in the JD-R sense
key_sources: Lesselroth Blake, Nooripour Roghieh, Srikasem Sirikanyawan MSc, Seephom Sunisa PhD, Viriyopase Atthaphon PhD, Phutrakool Phanupong PhD, Khowinthaseth Sirhavich MD, Narajeenron Khuansiri MD, MSc, CHSE, MHPE, ER-VIPE Study Group. (2025). Comparing the Effectiveness of Multimodal Learning Using Computer-Based and Immersive Virtual Reality Simulation–Based Interprofessional Education With Co-Debriefing, Medical Movies, and Massive Online Open Courses for Mitigating Stress and Long-Term Burnout in Medical Training: Quasi-Experimental Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/70726

article_title: Lots of Digital Files? How Digital Hoarding Is Related to the Academic Performance of University Students.
citation: Bravo-Adasme, N.; Cataldo, A.; Acosta-Antognoni, H.; Grandón, E.; Bravo, N.; Valdés, M. (2025). Lots of Digital Files? How Digital Hoarding Is Related to the Academic Performance of University Students. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph22081186
title: Job Demands–Resources theory applied to digital hoarding in academic settings
description: The Job Demands–Resources (JDR) model categorizes characteristics into demands, which require sustained effort and carry physiological and psychological costs, and resources, which reduce demands and foster growth and engagement. In this article it organizes the study of digital hoarding among students: demands include information overload and managing large volumes of files, while resources include technological skills, institutional support, and management tools. The authors find the health impairment process relevant: "high job demands may lead to strain and burnout (the health impairment process), whereas sufficient job resources can trigger motivational processes that result in increased engagement and positive outcomes".
requirements: Simultaneous consideration of demands and resources, which the authors state is its advantage over Karasek's demands–control model and the HERO model
constraints: The authors state the framework shows limitations for emerging phenomena: the nonsignificant digital hoarding–engagement link challenges the assumption that high demands generally harm motivational outcomes among digital natives
examples: The article models digital hoarding as a demand whose health impairment route runs through burnout to lower academic performance in a sample of Chilean university students
key_sources: Bravo-Adasme, N.; Cataldo, A.; Acosta-Antognoni, H.; Grandón, E.; Bravo, N.; Valdés, M. (2025). Lots of Digital Files? How Digital Hoarding Is Related to the Academic Performance of University Students. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph22081186

article_title: The Bright Side of Grit in Burnout-Prevention: Exploring Grit in the Context of Demands-Resources Model among Chinese High School Students.
citation: Teuber Ziwen, Nussbeck Fridtjof W., Wild Elke. (2021). The Bright Side of Grit in Burnout-Prevention: Exploring Grit in the Context of Demands-Resources Model among Chinese High School Students. Child Psychiatry and Human Development, 52(3), 464–476. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-020-01031-3
title: Job Demands-Resources model extended with grit as a personal resource for Chinese school contexts
description: The study transfers the Job Demands-Resources model to Chinese high schools, treating perceived academic demands as strain-inducing and grit (consistency of interests and perseverance of effort) as a personal resource "functional in dealing with these tasks". The model posits dual processes: a health-impairment process from demands to burnout to negative outcomes, and a motivational process from resources to engagement to positive outcomes. This is the first attempt to apply the JD-R model in Chinese school contexts with grit integrated.
requirements: Applicable to student populations experiencing high academic demands; requires measures of demands, grit facets, exhaustion, engagement, and outcomes
constraints: The authors note the JD-R model originated in occupational contexts and that burnout theory originates in Western cultures; cross-cultural comparisons remain to be conducted
target_learning_goals: Understanding and preventing school burnout; supporting student well-being and engagement under high academic demands
examples: The final SEM controlled for sex, SES, and school type and explained 32% of variance in exhaustion, 48.2% in engagement, and 27.9% in life satisfaction
key_sources: Teuber Ziwen, Nussbeck Fridtjof W., Wild Elke. (2021). The Bright Side of Grit in Burnout-Prevention: Exploring Grit in the Context of Demands-Resources Model among Chinese High School Students. Child Psychiatry and Human Development, 52(3), 464–476. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-020-01031-3
